d: Shaped like a ring
r: Latin ānulāris “ring-shaped”, from ānulus “ring”
s: Reminding them that the annular wing is a very old aeronautical principle.
old_f: Happening once a year
Cancelled by law
Marked with fine lines
ety: From Latin ānulāris (“ring-shaped”); (possibly through French annulaire), from ānulus (“ring”).

d: Relevant and appropriate
r: A variant of german “having the same parents; related”
s: Yet this much is germane to the present inquiry.
old_f: Free of bacteria
Coarse and rustic
Of Teutonic descent
ety: A variant form of german (“having the same parents; related”), adapted in this sense in allusions to its use in Shakespeare's Hamlet (see quotations at germaine).

d: A guide who conducts and informs sightseers
r: Italian cicerone, after Cicero, the Roman orator
s: Ultimately their gazes all rested on his cicerone as most powerful member of the group.
old_f: A small bird that chirps at dusk
A stout walking stick of olive wood
A sweet liqueur flavored with cherries
ety: 1726, from Italian cicerone (surface analysis cicero + -one (augmentative)), from Latin Cicerōnem, form of Cicerō, agnomen of Marcus Tullius Cicero), the Roman orator, from cicer (“chickpea”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱiker- (“pea”). Possibly humorous reference to loquaciousness of guides.

d: Having or exerting a malignant influence
r: Latin maleficus
s: I would have liked to know whether he thought this was due to the climate, the diet, or simply malefic djinns.
old_f: Having a poor or faulty shape
Relating to men and boys
Lacking enough to eat
ety: From Latin maleficus.

d: A girl who behaves in a boyish manner
r: Probably Middle Dutch heyden “heathen”
s: A great, strong, heavy girl, a hoyden, not pretty, her face distinguished only by youth, by health.
old_f: A boy who sings in a cathedral choir
A woman who keeps a small inn
A man who herds goats in the hills
ety: Probably from Middle Dutch heyden (“heathen, gypsy”), heidin (Modern Dutch heiden).

d: Someone skilled in the transcription of speech (especially dictation)
r: Latin āmanuēnsis “secretary”, from ab- “from” + manus “hand”
s: I, his mere amanuensis, am left to do what little I can to keep the institution functioning.
old_f: Someone skilled in the handling of horses (especially racehorses)
Someone devoted to the study of ancient languages (especially Latin)
Someone employed in the making of gloves (especially in Italy)
ety: From Latin āmanuēnsis (“secretary”), from ab- (“from, off (of)”) + manus (“hand”) + -ensis (“of or from (a place)”), early 17th c.

d: Blatant or sensational promotion
r: Probably French houp-là “upsy-daisy”; first attested c. 1877
s: Campers enjoyed all of the traditional camp hoopla.
old_f: A stiff wide petticoat
A loud wheezing cough
A child’s spinning top
ety: Earlier houp-la, hoop la, first attested in c. 1877, probably from French houp-là, oup-là (“upsadaisy, upsy-daisy”), a cry to various animals close to humans like horses and dogs, of likely onomatopoeic origin (but see là). Compare interjections like whoop, ahoy, hoo.

d: A reward or payment
r: Old French guerdon, from Medieval Latin widerdōnum, literally ‘back-payment’
s: Verse, like the laurel its immortal meed, Should be the guerdon of a noble deed.
old_f: A garden enclosure
A city guard
A war cry
ety: From Middle English guerdon, guerdoun, gardone, from Old French guerdon, guerredon, guarredon, werdon, from Medieval Latin widerdōnum, alteration of widerlōnum, from West Germanic (whence Old High German widarlōn, Old English wiþerlēan), literally ‘back-payment’, with the second element assimilated to Latin dōnum (“gift”).

d: To agree or express agreement
r: Latin acquiescō, from ad + quiescō “to rest”
s: They were compelled to acquiesce in a government which they did not regard as just.
old_f: Gain possession of
Fall silent and still
Clear of all blame
ety: Borrowed from Middle French acquiescer, from Latin acquiescō; ad + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).

d: Someone or something that is abnormally large and powerful
r: Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew behemót, likely an intensive plural of behemá “beast”
s: The conduits and pipes like the circulatory system of some vast planetary behemoth.
old_f: Someone or something that is regarded as a bad omen
Someone or something that has been cast out of a group
Someone or something that moves with silent stealth at night
ety: From Middle English behemoth, bemoth, from Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew בְּהֵמוֹת (behemót). Most likely, the Hebrew word is an intensive plural of בְּהֵמָה (behemá, “beast”), from Proto-Semitic (compare Ge'ez ብህመ (bəhmä, “to be dumb, to be speechless”), Arabic ب ه م (b h m)). Some have instead suggested a borrowing from a hypothetical Egyptian pA-i-H-E1-mw (*pꜣ-jḥ-mw, “hippopotamus”, literally “the ox of the water”), from pꜣ (“definite article”) + jḥ (“ox, cattle”) + mw (“water”) in a direct genitive construction (for the pronunciation, compare the later Coptic descendants ⲡ- (p-) + ⲉϩⲉ (

d: Immoderately desirous of acquiring e.g. wealth
r: Latin avaritia “greed”, from avarus “greedy”
s: He was called a hard, avaricious, rapacious man, whose chief business was to enrich himself.
old_f: Immoderately fond of keeping birds
Varied in form or kind
Eager to fly or travel by air
ety: From Middle English avaricious, from Old French avaricieux, from avarice, from Latin avaritia (“greed”), from avarus (“greedy”), of avere (“crave, long for”).

d: A broad cartridge belt worn over the shoulder by soldiers
r: Middle French bandoulliere, from Catalan bandolera, from bàndol “band, faction”
s: We had each bandoliers of cartridges.
old_f: A stringed instrument played by wandering folk musicians
A colored scarf tied around the head by sailors
A thin strip of cloth wrapped around a wound
ety: From earlier form bandollier, from Middle French bandoulliere, from Catalan bandolera, feminine derivative of bandoler (“member of a band of men”), from Catalan bàndol (“band, faction, party”), from Old Spanish bando.

d: Having no known beginning and presumably no end
r: Latin sempiternus, from semper “always” + æternus “eternal”
s: Why not sempiternal Thou and I?
old_f: Having half the usual number of musical notes
Having the shape of a half circle or arch
Happening twice in every month of the year
ety: From Old French sempiternel, from Medieval Latin sempiternālis, from Latin sempiternus, a contraction of semperæternus, from semper (“always”) + æternus (“eternal”).

d: Unpredictably excitable (especially of horses)
r: Probably skite “to move lightly and hurriedly” + -ish
s: The dog likes people he knows, but he is skittish around strangers.
old_f: Lightly salted (especially of fish)
Narrowly pleated (especially of skirts)
Thinly sliced (especially of bread)
ety: Probably from skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction (Scotland, Northern England)”) + -ish; compare skitter.

d: A state or atmosphere of harmony or mutual civility and respect
r: Latin cōmitās
s: Comity and conciliation are a slog.
old_f: A state or condition of deep unconsciousness caused by illness or injury
A group or body of people chosen to manage a specific task
A situation or play that is lighthearted and meant to amuse an audience
ety: From Late Middle English comite (“association”), from Latin cōmitās.

d: Argue over petty things
r: Back-formation from pettifogger
s: Don't pettifog or we will soon grow weary.
old_f: Stroke a pet gently
Fill with thick mist
Fuss over small children
ety: Back-formation from pettifogger.

d: Speech you make to yourself
r: Late Latin sōliloquium, from sōlus “only, sole” + loquor “to speak”
s: At the end of the second act the main villain gave a soliloquy detailing his plans to attack the protagonist.
old_f: Time you spend by yourself
Rest you take at midday
A song sung by one voice
ety: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to speak”).

d: Personal state of isolation and anxiety resulting from a lack of social control and regulation
r: French anomie, from Greek anomía “lawlessness”, from a- “not” + nómos “law”
s: From adolescent traumas to adulthood indignities, their anomie has been overdetermined.
old_f: Personal loss of memory and identity resulting from a sudden shock or a blow to the head
Personal state of deep hostility and suspicion resulting from a long-running feud between families
Bodily state of weakness and pallor resulting from a lack of red blood cells in the blood
ety: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).

d: Painful grief
r: Middle English dolour “pain, anguish, grief”, from Anglo-Norman dolour
s: Mysterious rites of dolour and despair, Permitting not a breath or chant of prayer?
old_f: Golden coin
Rag doll
Wooden bowl
ety: From Middle English dolour (“physical pain, agony, suffering; painful disease; anguish, grief, misery, sorrow; grieving for sins, contrition; hardship, misery, trouble; cause of grief or suffering, affliction”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman dolour, Old French dolour, dolor, dulur (“pain”) (modern French douleur (“pain; distress”)), from Latin dolor (“ache, hurt, pain; anguish, grief, sorrow; anger, indignation, resentment”), from doleō (“to hurt, suffer physical pain; to deplore, grieve, lament”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide, split”)) + -or (suffix forming th

d: Hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists
r: Latin nostrum “ours”
s: After each day's work in the fields, Brown was given some nostrum and made to repeat the ordeal.
old_f: Ancient formula for turning base metals into gold; once sought by the alchemists
Imaginary river that carries the souls of the dead; once feared by the ancients
Secret signal used by sailors to warn of coming storms; once flown from masts
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin nostrum (“ours”), nominative neuter of noster (“our, ours”).

d: A window with glass louvers
r: French jalousie; a doublet of jealousy
s: Venetian blinds, jalousies, closed every window.
old_f: A feeling of envious suspicion
A sweet fruit jelly
A small wooden spoon
ety: Borrowed from French jalousie. Doublet of jealousy.

d: Walk or tramp about
r: Likely French trépasser “pass over or beyond”
s: After traipsing about in the fog they found the grave sure enough.
old_f: Set a snare for game
Weave into a braid
Pass over in silence
ety: Likely from French trépasser (“pass over or beyond”).

d: Someone employed in a stable to take care of the horses
r: A phonetic spelling of hostler, from the late 14th century
s: An ostler leading a large and passive work-horse out to the day's labour.
old_f: Someone employed in a kitchen to clean the pots and pans
Someone employed in a hall to welcome and seat the guests
Someone employed in a mill to grind the oats and barley
ety: Phonetic spelling of hostler, from late 14th century.

d: A frame made of two hoops; used for embroidering
r: French tambour “drum”, from Arabic ṭunbūr; a doublet of tabor
s: Recollect Lady Teazle when I saw you first—sitting at your tambour in a pretty figured linen gown—
old_f: A cap made of soft wool; worn by fishermen
A chest made of carved wood; used for storing linen
A tray made of beaten brass; used for serving tea
ety: Borrowed from French tambour (“drum”), from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr), from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور (tanbūr). Doublet of tabor and tanbur. Compare Armenian տաւիղ (tawiġ), and tabla.

d: Cause oneself to consider something
r: Old English beþenċan “to think upon, remind, consider”: be- + think
s: “Bethink you to outbreathe through your mouths, and you’ll be fine.”
old_f: Cause oneself to stammer or stutter
Cause someone to feel guilty
Cause a plant to grow thick
ety: From Middle English bethenken, bithenchen (“to think about, consider”) from Old English beþenċan, biþenċan (“to think upon, remind, consider, remember”), from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną; equivalent to be- + think. Akin to Old High German pidenchan (German bedenken), Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌲𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (biþagkjan), Dutch bedenken.

d: So thin as to transmit light
r: Greek diaphanḗs, from dia- “through” + phaínō “to shine, appear”
s: Adam requires a touch of feminine lace and a whisper of diaphanous silk.
old_f: So loud as to drown out speech
So thick as to resist cutting
So bright as to dazzle the eye
ety: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

d: A feeling of deep regret (usually for some misdeed)
r: Late Latin compunctionem “a pricking”, from compungere “to severely prick”
s: As for average U.S. consumers, they've shown little compunction about buying diamonds that fund bloody militias in Africa.
old_f: A mark of short pause (usually in a written sentence)
A sharp stabbing pain (usually in the side)
A formal agreement to share (usually a family inheritance)
ety: From Middle English compunccion, borrowed from Old French compunction, from Late Latin compunctionem (“a pricking”), from Latin compunctus, the past participle of compungere (“to severely prick”), from com- + pungere (“to prick”).

d: A sudden uncontrollable attack
r: Middle French paroxisme “period of worsening of a disease, attack”
s: When the paroxysm had passed it left him shaking.
old_f: A small parish church
An apparent contradiction
A gas that bleaches hair
ety: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Latin paroxismus, paroxysmus (“a fit; onset of a disease; violent impulse or sadness”), from Ancient Greek πᾰροξῠσμός (păroxŭsmós, “exasperation, irritation; severe fit of a disease”), from πᾰροξῡ́νω (păroxū́nō, “to irritate, provoke”) (from παρα- (para-, prefix meaning ‘parallel to but separate from o

d: Dwelling beneath the surface of the earth
r: Greek khthónios “in or under the ground”, from khthṓn “ground”
s: The Olympian religion is truly Olympian when it rests on Chthonian grounds.
old_f: Dwelling in the branches of tall trees
Relating to the color of storm clouds
Living on the shores of a great lake
ety: From Ancient Greek χθόνιος (khthónios, “in or under the ground”), from χθών (khthṓn, “ground”).

d: A confused multitude of things
r: Middle English welteren: welt + -er; akin to wallow
s: They use these words to express a welter of opinions on what they think is good or bad, right or wrong.
old_f: A raised mark left by a whip
A heavy blanket of humid heat
A small spring of fresh water
ety: From Middle English welteren, equivalent to welt + -er (frequentative suffix). Cognates include German Low German weltern (“to wallow; roll”), Old Norse velta (Danish vælte), German wälzen, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌻𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (waltjan). Akin to wallow and Latin volvō.

d: A sandal with a sole made of rope or rubber and a cloth upper part
r: French espadrille
s: She wore loose black silks and black espadrilles.
old_f: A sword with a blade made of steel or bronze and a carved bone handle
A pastry with a crust made of almonds or honey and a soft cream filling
A shawl with a fringe made of silk or wool and a lace trim along the edge
ety: Borrowed from French espadrille.

d: A violent hot sand-laden wind on the deserts of Arabia and North Africa
r: Arabic samūm “hot wind”, from samma “to poison”
s: Stephen's heart had withered up like a flower of the desert that feels the simoom coming from afar.
old_f: A slow sweet chant sung by caravan drivers on the long desert crossings
A thick hooded robe of wool worn by herdsmen in the mountains of the Atlas
A shallow salt lake that dries out each summer in the deserts of Persia
ety: From Arabic سَمُوم (samūm, “hot wind”), from سَمَّ (samma, “to poison”).

d: Suitable for the general public
r: Late Latin exōtericus, from Greek exōterikós “exterior, external, outside”
s: Writings of an exoteric nature.
old_f: Foreign and strikingly unusual
Known only to a select few
Lying beyond the outer edge
ety: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Exōtericus is borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερῐκός (exōterĭkós, “exterior, external, outside”, adjective), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō, “more exterior”) (the comparative form of ἔξω (éxō, “external, outer”) (ultimately from ἐκ (ek, “beyond; outside”, preposition), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out”)) + -τέρω (-térō) (an inflected form of -τερος (-teros, suffix forming comparative forms)) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix forming adjectives). The noun is derived

d: Free from slavery or servitude
r: Latin manūmittere, literally “send out from one’s hand”
s: Even when, as you shall hear later, she was manumitted, she never entirely lost.
old_f: Work by hand rather than machine
Fertilize soil with animal dung
Govern or direct an estate
ety: From Middle English manumitten, from Latin manūmittere, from pre-Classical Latin manū ēmittere (literally “send out from one’s hand”).

d: A stubborn person of arbitrary or arrogant opinions
r: French doctrinaire, from doctrine + -aire
s: Or, shall we play the doctrinaire, and hint that at thirty-four the tides of life are calmer.
old_f: A young doctor in training at a large hospital
A small book of prayers and hymns for children
A careful collector of rare and ancient coins
ety: Borrowed from French doctrinaire, from doctrine + -aire.

d: Having no cause or apparent cause
r: Latin fortuītus “happening by chance”, from fors “chance, luck”
s: Was it love, she wondered, or a mere fortuitous combination of happy thoughts and sensations?
old_f: Having strong walls or defences
Having great wealth or riches
Having a strong or bitter flavor
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin fortuītus (“happening by chance, accidental, random, fortuitous”), from *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus (suffix forming adjectives). *Fortu- is thought to be from *fortus, from fors (“chance, luck”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns). Doublet of fortuity.

d: Anger produced by some annoying irritation
r: Middle French vexacion “anxiety, mental distress”
s: He clenched his fists in vexation and looked up at her impetuously.
old_f: A banner carried in a procession
A curve that bulges outward
A swelling caused by insect bites
ety: From Late Middle English vexacioun, vexation (“physical suffering; act of inflicting trouble (specifically through unjustified legal action); anxiety, mental distress; mental disturbance”), from Anglo-Norman vexacion, vexation, Middle French vexacion, vexation (“distress, suffering; harassment (specifically through unjustified legal action)”), and Old French vexacion, vexation (“distress, suffering; harassment”) (modern French vexation), and from their etymon Latin vexātiō (“shaking or similar violent movement; (causing of) agitation, distress, suffering; harassment, persecution; trouble”), fr

d: Not tractable; difficult to manage or mold
r: In- + tractable
s: Work—bureaucratic work in particular—poses a series of intractable dilemmas that often demand compromises with traditional moral beliefs.
old_f: Not traceable; impossible to follow or find
Not breakable; strong enough to resist force
Not drinkable; unsafe to swallow or taste
ety: From in- + tractable.

d: Make off with belongings of others
r: Anglo-Norman purloigner “to put far away”; a doublet of prolong
s: Had from his wakeful custody purloined The guarded gold.
old_f: Cut meat from along the spine
Knit in a raised ribbed stitch
Make clean and free of sin
ety: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.

d: In an advanced stage of pregnancy
r: Latin gravidus “laden, pregnant”, from gravis “heavy”
s: One slender hand was raised in a graceful gesture gravid with meaning.
old_f: Covered with a layer of grit
In a state of serious danger
Gray and grizzled with age
ety: From Latin gravidus (“laden, pregnant”), from gravis (“heavy”).
